messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald is a 67-year-old European American school principal, married for over three decades, who presented for an initial psychological assessment approximately four months after surviving a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. He was driving home from a late administrative meeting when a vehicle ran a red light and struck his car broadside at high speed. The impact was sudden and total — the shriek of metal, the explosive crack of airbags, the sensation of the world spinning sideways. He was extracted by emergency personnel and hospitalised overnight with chest injuries and a concussion. By all external measures, he recovered. Internally, he has not.

Gerald reports that his memories of the collision do not behave like ordinary memories. He cannot narrate the event in any coherent sequence — when asked to describe what happened, he falls silent and shakes his head, saying the words simply will not come. What does come, unbidden and with terrible regularity, is the film: a loop of sensation and image — the flash of headlights, the sound of impact, the smell of deployed airbag — that replays as though the event is happening at this very moment. He has woken his wife reaching out to brace against a dashboard that is not there.

These intrusive memories are reliably detonated by the world around him. The slam of a locker in the school corridor, a raised voice during a staff meeting, the sight of two cars pulling too close together in the car park — each of these collapses the distance between then and now. Gerald has come to understand this as evidence that he cannot trust his own nervous system, and this conviction — that he has been permanently and fundamentally altered — sits at the centre of how he now interprets everything. He is certain someone more capable, more composed, would not have been in that intersection at that moment. The world, he believes, is no longer a place that follows reasonable rules; danger arrives without warning and without logic, and he is uniquely ill-equipped to survive it. These appraisals have made the triggers more potent still: because he already believes catastrophe is imminent, the sound of shouting in a hallway or the sight of a car braking sharply does not merely startle him — it confirms what he already knows, and the memories flood back with renewed force.

The threat he carries is constant and exhausting. He cannot fall asleep without lying rigid for an hour, listening. He cannot sit in a staff meeting without monitoring every sound. When a parent's phone call takes longer than expected to connect, he is immediately certain something terrible has occurred. This unrelenting state of vigilance feeds directly back into his appraisals — the fact that he cannot relax, even in his own office, feels to Gerald like proof that the damage is permanent, that he is broken in a way that will not heal. And the hypervigilance itself makes the triggers everywhere: loud noises that once meant nothing now arrive as alarms, and the memories follow within seconds.

To manage all of this, Gerald has constructed a set of strategies that have quietly made things worse. He has been avoiding going to work as much as his role will allow — arriving late, delegating morning assemblies, leaving before the end-of-day rush in the car park. This avoidance has not gone unnoticed; two senior staff members have raised concerns about his absence from key decisions, and he is aware his authority is eroding. He forces himself to think only positively, suppressing any thought that touches the accident, which leaves the memories with nowhere to go and ensures they return with greater force. He has been eating excessively in the evenings — a habit that crept up over the first weeks and has now become a nightly ritual of distraction. Each of these strategies, in their own way, sustains the belief that the world is too dangerous to engage with directly, and that he is too damaged to cope — beliefs that keep his threat system primed and his triggers hair-trigger sensitive.

What finally brought Gerald to seek help was a morning three weeks ago when he could not make himself walk into the school building. He stood in the car park for twenty minutes and drove home. He told his wife that evening, for the first time, how frightened he was — not of the school, but of never being himself again. That is what he most fears: not another accident, but that the man who walked into that intersection is gone, and that no one, including him, has noticed yet.
